evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Retroactive restriction of 1885–1890 police-court usage solely to employed workers.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether Reitman recorded earlier oral Hobo College / I.W.W. phrasing prior to February 1908.

claims.short_label: Proposed delocutive derivation from Northwestern / rail greeting call 'Ho, boy!' / 'Ho! Bo!'
claims.statement: Delocutive nominalization of an itinerant/rail greeting call ('Ho, boy!' / 'Ho! Bo!' / 'Obo' -> 'hoboys' / 'hobo') best fits the 1885–1894 salute/countersign witnesses, nautical vocative 'bo', and H. R. Jeffrey's 1920 Oregon Short Line report, though pre-1885 phonetic reduction remains unrecorded in real time.
claims.rationale: Earliest attestations treat 'Obo'/'Hobo' as a hail/countersign (CLM-2300-002, 004, 005), Smyth (1867, CERT-2300-308) supplies vocative 'BO', Flynt/Mencken (309) confirm ''bo < hobo', and Jeffrey (1920, 307) recalls 1880s OSL mail clerks calling 'Ho, boy!' -> 'hoboys'.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Convergence of earliest 1885–1894 greeting/countersign attestations with delocutive 'Ho, boy!' / 'Ho! Bo!' formation.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Contemporary pre-November 1885 documentary proof of oral 'Ho, boy!' -> 'hobo' reduction.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Relative roles of Twin Cities camp workers versus Pacific Northwest rail clerks before November 1885.

limitations: Jeffrey's 1920 Dialect Notes report is 30-year-retrospective testimony.
resolution_criteria: Locate pre-November 1885 Northwestern print or manuscript witnesses spelling the itinerant hail 'Ho, bo!' or 'hoboys'.

evidence.reason: 1920 Jeffrey Dialect Notes OSL 'Ho, boy!' -> 'hoboys' testimony plus 1877 hail.

claims.short_label: Weakened scholarly/activist derivations from agricultural 'hoe-boy' and Northern English 'hawbuck'
claims.statement: Deriving 'hobo' from agricultural 'hoe-boy' (Klein 1922 / Anderson 1923) or Northern English 'hawbuck'/'hawbaw' (Liberman) remains inconclusive due to zero migratory-farmhand tokens across 24 nineteenth-century farm manuals and phonological/semantic divergence on 'hawbuck'.
claims.rationale: Pre-1890 agricultural checks find only 1818 mission schoolboys and an 1885 Georgia joke before 1920s Hobo College advocacy (CERT-2300-311, 312), while Cumberland/British 'hawbuck' ('bumpkin'; NJ 1865 'tomboy', CERT-2300-313, 314) leaves '-k' loss and /oʊ-oʊ/ unexplained.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Empirical lexical and phonological gaps weakening both 'hoe-boy' and 'hawbuck' without treating either as a folk backronym.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Absolute impossibility of secondary harvest-worker reinterpretation.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether unindexed 1870s–1880s wheat-belt broadsides ever applied 'hoe-boy' to adult migrants.

limitations: Evaluated respectfully as weakened hypotheses ('inconclusive') per DRAgNEt register standards.
resolution_criteria: Locate pre-1885 Western print attesting adult migratory 'hoe-boy' or transitional '*hawbo'.

evidence.reason: 0 migratory-worker 'hoe-boy' hits across 24 farm manuals (only 1818 schoolboys & 1885 pun).
1923 Anderson summary of Klein's 1922 Hobo College 'hoe-boy' theory.
1902 Wright EDD 'hawbuck' and 1896 Dialect Notes NJ sense 'tomboy'.
